BOI.excerpt: The short-wave ridge that kept the weekend dry will begin to break down Monday, as another low digs down the coast of British Columbia and into the northwest CONUS. Uncertainty remains on the exact timing of when this low will impact our area.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread precipitation continuing through the morning. A 10-20% chance of thunderstorms in SW-Idaho early this morning.
- Windy today behind a cold front. Gusts to 30-40 mph this morning then 20-35 mph this afternoon.
- Cool and dry this weekend, frost possible Saturday and Sunday mornings.
- Unsettled pattern setting in again late Monday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Rain showers will continue overnight into Friday morning as the upper low moves northeast over our area. Model soundings hold on to elevated instability prior to a cold frontal passage. This elevated instability will give way to a 10-20% chance of thunderstorms across southwest Idaho early this morning. With earlier activity saturating the low levels, and the nocturnal stable layer in place, the wind threat has diminished greatly, with brief heavy rain the primary hazard with thunderstorms. The Flash Flood Watch will continue this morning for recent burn scars in the Boise Mountains. The threat of thunderstorms will diminish behind a cold front by the afternoon, with precipitation tapering off from W-E through the afternoon.

The aforementioned cold front is currently making it's way into eastern Oregon, pushing through SW Idaho through the morning. This front will bring W-NW winds with widespread gusts to 30-40 mph. Locally higher gusts to 45-55 mph will be seen in windier portions of Baker and Malhuer counties (including portions of I-84 where wind will be channeled through Baker Valley), through sunrise. Winds will taper off slightly as the front moves out this afternoon, but gusts to 20-35 mph will persist for much of the area. Snow levels behind the cold front will lower to 4.5-6 kft MSL in E-Oregon and 6-8 kft in SW-Idaho. The lowering snow- levels coincide with the precipitation tapering off, with just minor accumulations expected over higher peaks. Temperatures this afternoon will be quite a bit cooler than yesterday, with high temps generally in the 50s across lower elevations. Dry air and a shortwave ridge moving in behind this front will result in skies clearing from W-E across the area this afternoon into the overnight hours.

After the last of the precipitation moves out of the area Friday night, the aforementioned ridge will bring dry conditions for the rest of the weekend. Frost will be possible Saturday morning in lower elevations. However, breezy winds will persist which may hinder frost development outside of some localized areas. While Sunday morning will generally be slightly warmer, calmer winds will likely increase the frost risk in lower elevations. With clear skies and low level moisture supplemented by the rain showers, areas of fog may also develop in lower elevations.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The short-wave ridge that kept the weekend dry will begin to break down Monday, as another low digs down the coast of British Columbia and into the northwest CONUS. Uncertainty remains on the exact timing of when this low will impact our area. Ensemble mean 500mb heights have it passing our area late Monday into Tuesday, which is reflected in the forecast with increasing precipitation chances Monday afternoon, peaking overnight Monday. The best chances of precipitation will come across higher terrain of SW-Idaho, with a 55-65% chance in Valley County, elsewhere north of the Snake Plain will carry a 30-50% chance. With this system bringing cooler temperatures and lowering snow levels, elevations above 6.5 kft MSL have a 35-60% chance of seeing at least an inch of snow between 6pm MDT Monday through 6pm MDT Tuesday; elevations above 7kft MSL have a 30-50% chance of seeing greater than 2 inches over the same period. Uncertainty increases beyond Tuesday with the pattern evolution. However, with the Grand Ensemble resolving zonal flow before general troughing, a cool and unsettled pattern is likely to continue. The CPC outlooks seem to agree, with our area highlighted with near normal temperatures and leaning towards above normal in regard to precipitation.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Into the long term our temperatures will drop several degrees below average under a colder airmass with some increasing chances for precipitation, primarily for our eastern zones this time, with temperatures then warming to near average by the middle of the work week under brief clearing.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A High Wind Warning has been issued for much of Carbon County and portions of Albany County from 5AM to 3PM today.
- Above average temperatures will continue today, but a weekend system will drop temperatures near to below average.
- Precipitation is possible this afternoon through Sunday, with the potential for frozen precipitation outside of the mountains Sunday morning.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday into Wednesday, but next Pacific system will be approaching from the Pacific Northwest by the middle of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The upper-level trough that has been moving towards the region over the past few days will start to significantly impact western portions of the CWA starting this morning. The upper-level trough is currently located over Nevada and Oregon, with a modest jet developing as the ridge starts to move off towards the Mississippi River Valley. The upper-level system will strengthen this afternoon and evening as split flow develops over the Intermountain West. A much stronger 250mb jet is anticipated to develop overhead this afternoon and evening. A few lobes of 500mb vorticity eject out ahead of the incoming trough this afternoon, adding to the synoptic forcing across the region. Much of the area will be under the right entrance region of the upper-level jet into the overnight hours, favoring increased forcing. The 700mb trough currently looks to remain on track, with a northeasterly jump from northern Nevada into southern Montana this morning. The trough will deepen slightly this morning, resulting in strong height gradients across much of the area and a 50kt, southwesterly jet across western portions of the CWA. GFS Omega fields suggest modest downward motion across western Carbon County with the increasing 700mb jet overhead, favoring downward acceleration. The surface pressure gradient looks to increase this morning and afternoon for this same area as the surface low over eastern Montana deepens throughout the day. While the strong 700mb jet will quickly weaken into the afternoon hours as the 700mb trough continues to move quickly to the northeast, this will not occur before very strong winds develop across western Carbon County. In-house Random Forest guidance suggests around a 20% chance for high winds at Rawlins so, with recent model runs starting to increase the 700mb jet this morning, a High Wind Warning has been issued for much of Carbon County and portions of Albany County, including the Arlington/Elk Mountain wind prone zone. Sustained winds between 30 and 35mph are expected for much of the mid-morning hours with gusts likely between 55 and 60mph, though a rouge gust up to 65mph cannot be completely ruled out at some of the wind prone locations.

As far as precipitation is concerned for Friday into Saturday morning, southwesterly surface flow across Carbon County will not only produce strong winds, but will also favor upslope development across the Sierra Madre Range, with precipitation starting to push northeastward Friday evening into the overnight hours. 700mb temperatures will start to decrease this afternoon into the 2 to 4C range across Carbon County, while remaining quite warm east of this, in the 6 to 8C range. As a result, precipitation across the Sierra Madre Range looks to start as mostly rain, with warmer 700mb temperatures not supporting snow development. However, into the overnight hours and early Saturday morning, 700mb temperatures drop to at or below 0C across the mountains. This would favor rain switching to snow Saturday morning, though significant accumulation is not anticipated. Any precipitation outside of the mountains should remain primarily rain, as recent model runs suggest a slightly warmer system than originally thought.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: No major changes, please see previous discussion...

Into the long term our temperatures will drop several degrees below average under a colder airmass with some increasing chances for precipitation, primarily for our eastern zones this time, with temperatures then warming to near average by the middle of the work week under brief clearing. The upper level pattern will see the northern trough quickly accelerating eastwards, leaving us under southwesterly flow aloft from a brief finger of weak transient ridging that will quickly be erased by low pressure slowly progressing across the Four Corners region. This will then become our main weather feature through Monday before finally sliding eastwards into the Central Plains, with another transient ridge building on Tuesday that will briefly hold the region before another Pacific low moves into the Pacific Northwest and then starts to knock on our doorstep by Wednesday into Thursday. Under this pattern, we should see surface flow begin to weaken by later Saturday and continue into the early part of next week as the strongest part of the jet remains just south and west of the forecast area. With this flow, the best moisture will remain just outside of our forecast area to the east as well. That being said, PWAT values will still be on the higher side even for our area by around 0.15-0.25 inch, and scattered shower activity is expected from Saturday afternoon and continuing through Monday evening before exiting the region. The highest QPF amounts should align with the best moisture for the southeastern portions of the Nebraska Panhandle, but some meager moisture should occur across most of the forecast area east of the Laramie Range. Morning lows both Sunday and Monday could also allow for this to mix with snow, but don't expect noteworthy winter accumulations at this time. As conditions finally clear later Monday into Tuesday and the transient ridge moves in, 700mb temperatures will warm back into the 5-8 C range, allowing surface temperatures to rise back to near average in the 50- 60 degree range. Tightening pressure gradients from the approaching Pacific system will start to increase westerly to southwesterly winds again for our western zones on Tuesday and Wednesday, but otherwise expect conditions to be a bit more uneventful as precipitation chances dwindle outside of the high terrain for the middle of the week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate the region by Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding is ongoing across portions of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado, and is expected to continue through Saturday.
- Many rivers will experience their crest Friday or Saturday.
- Isolated to scattered showers and storms are expected Friday and Saturday. They will be capable of producing moderate to heavy rainfall that could result in additional flooding.
- A few storms may be capable of producing strong winds and large hail Friday and Saturday afternoon.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The main low pressure responsible for all of the recent rainfall is currently located over Nevada and California. This has kept us in southwest flow aloft. Most of the deep tropical moisture has pushed east of the area with the exception of south central Colorado. This is where isolated to scattered showers and storms will be possible mainly this afternoon. These showers will be capable of producing strong winds, hail and heavy rainfall. The main concern is more rainfall for this region, which is already experience flooding. Given the ground is very saturated it might not take much more rainfall to cause additional flooding. Tonight and tomorrow the low pressure begins to approach from southern California. As that happens it will draw moisture back into the area. Therefore we will see an uptick in showers and storms starting tonight and continuing tomorrow. The coverage during this time frame expands to locations mainly along and south of I-70. This means additional rainfall for places that have already experienced excessive rainfall. The rainfall amounts through Sunday are expected to range from 0.5-1.0 inches along the highway 160 corridor with slightly higher amounts in the mountains and lower amounts outside of southwest Colorado. Training storms could result in 1-3 inches, which could result in more flooding and a continuation of ongoing flooding. The low pressure lifts overhead on Sunday so expect more showers across the area. However these showers should be relatively light compared to the past few days. Conditions dry out on Monday as the low pressure lifts out over the Plains.

As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate the region by Monday. Because of this, we will be seeing cooler than normal temperatures, with the potential for overnight lows to drop below freezing for a couple hours at a time. Keep in mind, this is still relatively far out, so confidence remains low on this matter.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Monday through Thursday...Upper low weakens, opens and tracks east across CO as an open wave on Monday, with just some lingering isolated to low end scattered showers across the CWA.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flood Watch remains in effect through this afternoon for the eastern San Juan mountains and the Upper Rio Grande Valley, with stream/river flooding and rock/mud slides possible.
- Rainfall starting to diminish across the higher terrain through this morning, then strong thunderstorms possible along the southern border and eastern plains later this afternoon.
- Cooler and wetter weather areawide this weekend, with gradual warming and drying for the upcoming week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Pacific low pressure system centered over NV was continuing to produce rounds of moderate to heavy rain along the Continental Divide overnight, with the focus area continuing to be the southwest mts where 3 to 4 inches of rain have already fallen in the past 24 hrs, and local emergency management are dealing with an ongoing flooding threat. The area will likely receive up to an inch of additional rainfall before the night is through. Overnight low temps are forecast to drop into the 40s for the high valleys, which they are already at, and upper 40s to upper 50s for the plains.

Today and tonight...Models are holding onto previous forecast solution, with the upper low pushing north into MT through the day while a secondary piece of energy drops south across NV. Tonight the northern low weakens and pushes east across MT, forcing a cold front south across eastern WY. At the same time, the southern low closes off across southern CA and AZ, continuing strong south-southwest flow across the Four Corners and CO. All the models are indicating a dramatic drop off in rainfall across the forecast area through the first half of the day, with additional QPF amounts across the southern mts amounting to around .20 of an inch, and the Flood Watch for the sw mts will be allowed to expire at 6 PM. By the afternoon and early evening, the focus for shower and storm activity shifts to the southern border and farther east, with CAPE of 500-1200 j/kg combining with 40-50 kts of bulk shear. SPC has painted a Marginal area for severe thunderstorms along the southern border and up across a portion of the eastern plains, with the main threat for the stronger storms being strong wind gusts up to 60 mph and hail up to one inch in diameter. This will be the last really warm day for the eastern plains as temps once again climb into the 70s to around 80F, while the high valleys climb into the 60s.
Those living or traveling across the southwest mountains and the San Luis Valley should continue to stay weather aware today, and have multiple ways to receive weather warnings.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday and Sunday...A cold front pushes south into eastern CO Saturday morning, while the southern closed low moves up across AZ and reaches the Four Corners by Sat night. This will produce strong south to southwest flow, this time situated across the eastern half of the state. Widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected on Saturday, with excessive rainfall amounts possible for the eastern plains, and new accumulating snow for the mts as snow levels drop to around 9000 ft late that night. SPC currently has just painted much of the plains in General Thunder, but I would not be surprised to see a Marginal enter the plains on upcoming updates due to impressive shear. On Sunday the upper low weakens slightly and tracks east into CO, continuing to bring rain and storm chances to the plains, and additional light snow to the mts. This will be the coolest days of the forecast period, with highs in the upper 40s to mid 50s for the high valleys both days. For the plains, look for 50s to around 60F for Saturday, then 50s for Sunday.

Monday through Thursday...Upper low weakens, opens and tracks east across CO as an open wave on Monday, with just some lingering isolated to low end scattered showers across the CWA. Temporary broad ridging aloft moves across the region for Tuesday, then brisk southwest flow aloft from a disturbance passing by to the north for Wednesday and Thursday. Plan on a gradual warming and drying trend through the week, with a return to seasonal temperatures. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Models then have some uncertainty with the exact pattern evolution through much of the week. There is some agreement in another trough brushing by the region, but differences in exactly how and when.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Showers continue Friday across portions of northern Utah and southwest Wyoming as the core of a broad low shifts in. Showers then redevelop across portions of southern and eastern Utah Saturday and Sunday.
- Disturbances will continue to ripple through the region through the upcoming week, maintaining periods of unsettled weather with occasional dry days mixed in.
- Below normal to seasonable temperatures persist into the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Morning satellite water vapor loop shows the core of a large scale trough pivoting into northern Utah through the Great Basin. Lingering moisture combined with synoptic forcing from the trough will result in scattered shower activity persisting across portions of northern Utah and southwest Wyoming through the day Friday. A few embedded thunderstorms may also develop during the afternoon and early evening hours. Overall though, not anticipating this activity to be overly impactful especially in comparison to the prior days. Other than that, just a chilly day across the area with afternoon highs around 5-10 degrees below seasonal normal, and watching as streams and basins in southern Utah gradually drain.

Moving into Saturday, a portion of the trough will become cutoff from the mean flow and sink through Utah and into the Desert Southwest. This will allow for a continuation of cooler and somewhat unsettled conditions, with showers and a few thunderstorms redeveloping across southeast Utah by Saturday morning. With the slow progression of the low, unsettled conditions will then continue on into the overnight hours and spread to areas further north across the eastern half of Utah into Sunday. Activity will finally wane late Sunday evening on through the overnight hours as the low departs eastward.

Monday is favored to be a drier day as a brief shortwave ridge shifts through overhead. In addition to the stable conditions, this will also allow temperatures to rebound back to near seasonable normal.

Models then have some uncertainty with the exact pattern evolution through much of the week. There is some agreement in another trough brushing by the region, but differences in exactly how and when. For now, the best agreement is in the Tuesday to Wednesday time frame, with best chance of precipitation noted across northern Utah to southwest Wyoming. Thereafter models support something in the way of a fairly dry zonal flow to building ridge. If the ridge scenario becomes more favored, then would expect to see forecast temperatures also nudge upwards.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: A moisture-laden storm arrives in Colorado on Wednesday, bringing early-season avalanche concerns to steep, snow-covered slopes. Nearly every fall, small avalanches catch eager snow riders, late-season hikers, and hunters off guard. If you are traveling through the high country over the next few days, exercise caution on steep, snow-covered terrain.

For Wednesday and Thursday, in areas with snow already on the ground, rain falling on the early snowpack increases the potential for Wet Loose avalanches. From Thursday through the weekend, as new snow accumulates and wind-drifted snow obscures the ground cover, dry slab and loose avalanches will become a threat at the highest elevations. It doesn't take much snow on steep grassy slopes, rock slabs, or remnant snowfields for slides to occur.
We will update the Statewide Avalanche Conditions as necessary. On November 1, 2026, we will resume our daily weather and avalanche forecasts.
We will update the Field Report and Avalanche Observations as information comes in, so please send us your observations.
An impressive tropical moisture stream takes aim at the Southern Mountains this week.

Wednesday & Thursday: During the early parts of the storm, precipitation will start as rain. Under specific storm cells dropping high-intensity precipitation and at the highest elevations, you can expect a few inches of snow by Thursday morning.

Thursday Night & Friday: A cold front will drop temperatures and snow levels. Expect 6 to 12+ inches of snow above treeline in the San Juan Mountains by Friday morning. The Central Mountains may see several inches in favored areas, with lighter accumulation further north.

Saturday through Monday: A closed low-pressure system crosses the Four Corners region, bringing additional snow. Depending on the storm's exact track, the Southern Mountains could see over 6 additional inches, while the Central and Northern Mountains can expect up to 6 inches.
The storm moves east on Tuesday, bringing a short-lived high-pressure ridge before another potential storm arrives for Halloween weekend.

You can get up-to-date point weather forecasts on our Weather Forecasts page by clicking on the map or searching for a location. You can also get model forecasts on our Point Forecasts page and Model Forecast page. You can check current weather conditions across Colorado on our Weather Stations page.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
